newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany mulls petrol tax to plug fiscal hole.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany mulls petrol tax to plug fiscal hole.

text.p: Germany's coalition government is mulling a petrol tax hike to plug a financing hole blown by the opposition Social Democrats' (SPD) veto of parts of its 1997 tax bill, coalition sources said on Wednesday.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel is seeking ways to fill a multi-billion mark shortfall which will result next year from a rise in child benefits and the scrapping of a wealth tax.
But he says Germany would still meet the Maastricht treaty's debt and deficit criteria next year to qualify for the scheduled launch of the single European currency in 1999.
Parliamentary and party leaders from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrat (CDU/CSU) coalition discussed the possibility of the petrol tax rise at the chancellor's office on Wednesday.
"We are furiously calculating and discussing," one source said, adding the coalition would await what savings measures the SPD proposes before deciding on the petrol tax increase.
Germany will overshoot Maastricht's budget deficit ceiling of three percent of GDP this year, but Waigel is sticking to his 2.5 percent target next year despite the tax bill setback.

The tax bill is part of a 70 billion mark ($45.4 billion) austerity plan intended to reduce the tax burden and stimulate job creation in Germany, suffering from unemployment stuck near four million despite an accelerating economic recovery.
But it always ran the risk of being wrecked by an SPD wielding a majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament enabling it to block tax plans.
The stalemate means the wealth tax, ruled unconstitutional by a court, will be abolished from the start 1997 -- hitting regional governments with a revenue loss of nine billion marks.
Failure to agree also means a 20 mark increase in monthly child benefits to 220 marks will go ahead automatically -- at a cost of 5.5 billion marks -- which Waigel had wanted to defer.
The losses will be partly offset by changes in inheritance tax and other revisions which should still become law. But that still leaves a hefty gap to close.

The Munich Abendzeitung newspaper said Waigel's Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), Kohl's sister party, was mulling a petrol tax hike of over 10 pfennigs a litre. But spokesman Maximilian Schoeberl said no decision had yet been taken.

SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss hit out at Waigel for contemplating asking motorists to pay up seven billion marks in extra petrol taxes to finance policies which were "getting increasingly out of control".
Petrol taxes have more than doubled since 1988 to 1.13 marks a litre, Poss said in a statement.

And junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) will not support the petrol tax increase -- or a possible hike in value-added tax which Kohl hinted at over the summer, party leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told German radio.

The tax deadlock also means that Waigel will not be able to abolish a capital trading tax, seen by businesses as hindering enterprise and investment. It will now have to be imposed in depressed eastern Germany.
The tax juggling could not come at a worse time for Germany as it seeks to profile itself as the stable cornerstone of Europe's project for monetary union.
Kohl hosted Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar on Tuesday to discuss Madrid's chances of qualifying for EMU, and has invited Italian premier Romano Prodi to dinner on Thursday.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
